source.title: Can Dialects Be Steered Like Languages? Sparse Neurons and Distributed Directions in Arabic LLMs
source.authors: K. Elozeiri; Mervat T. Abassy; Omar Kallas; Fahim Dalvi; Preslav Nakov; Kentaro Inui; Nadir Durrani

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses LAPE-based neuron selection and activation-vector steering to control dialect generation. Its results concern dialect control and neuron-subspace coverage, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs or have coherent jobs.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure polysemanticity, unrelated token/context responses, or whether mixed inputs share a feature. Its dialect-neuron coverage and steering outcomes are relevant adjacent findings, recorded as none of the claim versions. Reported findings from prior work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study selects dialect-associated MLP neurons with LAPE and steers them or residual vectors to control Arabic dialect generation. It never measures whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, how common polysemantic neurons are, or what causes them. Its coverage and steering results concern dialect localization versus distribution, a related but different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that dialect information is both sparse and distributed: LAPE neurons capture only part of the residual dialect direction, and vector steering gives more reliable dialect control, including from MSA prompts where neuron steering fails.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not use a polysemanticity identification or explanation-scoring recipe; it applies LAPE selection and activation-vector steering to Arabic dialect control.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering outcomes vary by model, dialect, layer, steering coefficient, and number of steered tokens; the paper reports different layer profiles and dialect-specific quality trade-offs.

fits_no_version.finding: LAPE-selected dialect neurons (<1% of MLP dims) span 4.7–20.6% of residual dialect directions. Several dialects are enriched over matched random subsets, but most of each direction lies outside the neuron subspace.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Arabic dialect features in these LLMs are only partly captured by sparse selective MLP neurons and are largely distributed in residual space.

fits_no_version.finding: Dialect neuron sets overlap strongly across spoken dialects (Jaccard about 0.40–0.55 on average) but weakly with MSA (0.09–0.14). This suggests neurons are shared across related varieties.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dialect-selective neurons are shared across related dialects rather than being dialect-exclusive.

fits_no_version.finding: Neuron steering fails to induce dialect from MSA prompts, while vector steering succeeds.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse neuron steering reinforces but cannot induce dialect generation.

record.problems: Evidence is limited to two Arabic-centric instruction-tuned models and selected Arabic dialects. Coverage is a residual-subspace measure, not a direct measurement of neuron meanings or polysemanticity. The paper notes that the relationship between localized neuron representations and distributed residual features is only partially understood.
record.rows_left_out: Not extracted: detailed mono-dialect steering scores for all methods, dialects, and metrics (Tables 1–2 and Appendices F/I), vector steering scores for each MSA-prompt target dialect (Table 3), and the neuron/vector ablation sweeps (Appendices A–B). These report dialect-generation outcomes rather than polysemanticity or unrelated-input responses.

untested.parts: Share of LM MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how it varies by layer. The layer distribution reported covers only dialect-selective neurons.
Superposition or capacity as a cause.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization or noise.
Effects of architecture, activation function or regularization on the polysemantic share.
Whether mixed neurons share one feature.
How the measurement choice affects polysemanticity judgments.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'feature entanglement at the neuron level' motivation is mentioned but not measured. Neuron cross-dialect overlap (Fig 2b) concerns related, not unrelated, inputs, so it does not bear on V2 or V6. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Vision-model neurons and the InceptionV1 examples.
Whether a large share of transformer MLP neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, and how that share varies by layer.
Whether polysemanticity is caused by sparse-feature superposition or capacity pressure.
Polysemanticity from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
Changes in polysemantic-neuron share due to activation function, architecture, or regularization, including SoLU or modern convnets, and any performance trade-off.
Whether canonical polysemantic neurons detect a shared feature or related jobs, or whether truly unrelated mixtures are rare.
Whether polysemanticity judgments depend on activation range examined or explanation-scoring method.
